section.title: Gethsemane and the Arrest
section.sectionRationale: Jesus foretells that all will fall away and Peter will deny Him. In Gethsemane He wrestles in agony with the cup set before Him, submitting fully to the Father's will, then is betrayed with a kiss, refuses rescue, and is arrested as the disciples flee.
section.thesis: Facing the cup of God's judgment, Jesus is overwhelmed with sorrow yet surrenders wholly to the Father's will, and He goes to His betrayal and arrest not as a victim but as the willing Son who fulfills the Scriptures and could summon legions of angels but will not.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the prediction that all will fall away and Peter will deny; the agony and threefold prayer in Gethsemane; and the betrayal, the sword, and the arrest as the disciples flee.

verses.text: Then Jesus said to them, “This very night you will all fall away on account of Me. For it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’
But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”
Peter said to Him, “Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will.”
“Truly I tell you,” Jesus declared, “this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.”
Peter replied, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” And all the other disciples said the same thing.

units.label: Gethsemane
units.note: not as I will, but as You will

verses.text: Then Jesus went with His disciples to a place called Gethsemane, and He told them, “Sit here while I go over there and pray.”
He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee and began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed.
Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with Me.”
Going a little farther, He fell facedown and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this {{poterion|cup}} pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.”
Then Jesus returned to the disciples and found them sleeping. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” He asked Peter.
“{{gregoreo|Watch}} and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.”
A second time He went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your {{thelema|will}} be done.”
And again Jesus returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
So He left them and went away once more and prayed a third time, saying the same thing.
Then He returned to the disciples and said, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour is near, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!”

units.label: The betrayal and arrest
units.note: a kiss, a sword, and the Scriptures fulfilled

verses.text: While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests and elders of the people.
Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.”
Going directly to Jesus, he said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him.
“Friend,” Jesus replied, “do what you came for.” Then the men stepped forward, seized Jesus, and arrested Him.
At this, one of Jesus’ companions drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear.
“Put your sword back in its place,” Jesus said to him. “For all who draw the sword will die by the sword.
Are you not aware that I can call on My Father, and He will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels?
But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?”
At that time Jesus said to the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? Every day I sat teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me.
But this has all happened so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.

poterion.gloss: A cup. In the prophets the cup is the cup of God's wrath and judgment that the wicked must drink; in Gethsemane Jesus faces this cup, the judgment due to sinners, and prays that it might pass, yet resolves to drink it in the sinner's place.

gregoreo.gloss: To stay awake, be alert, keep watch. Jesus asks His friends to watch with Him and to watch and pray against temptation; their failure to stay awake exposes the weakness of the flesh even when the spirit is willing.

thelema.gloss: Will, what one desires or purposes. The center of Gethsemane is the surrender of Jesus' human will to the Father's: not as I will, but as You will, may Your will be done, the obedience by which He embraces the cross.

basic.context: On the way to the Mount of Olives, Jesus foretells that all the disciples will desert Him that night, quoting Zechariah about the struck Shepherd, and He warns Peter he will deny Him three times. In Gethsemane He is overwhelmed with sorrow and prays three times that the cup might pass, yet each time surrenders to the Father's will while His friends sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd and betrays Him with a kiss. A companion draws a sword, but Jesus stops him, refuses angelic rescue so the Scriptures may be fulfilled, and is arrested as all the disciples flee.
basic.hermeneutics: Gethsemane shows the genuine humanity of Jesus: real anguish, real prayer, real submission. The cup is not merely death but the judgment of God against sin. His refusal to summon angels shows the cross is chosen, not forced. The disciples' failure and flight fulfill His words and expose the weakness that only His faithfulness will redeem.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus faces the poterion, the cup of God's judgment, and prays it might pass. He asks His friends to gregoreo, to keep watch, but they sleep. And the heart of His prayer is thelema, the Father's will: not as I will, but as You will.
basic.typology: The struck Shepherd and scattered sheep fulfill Zechariah 13. The cup of wrath fulfills the prophetic image of the cup God's judgment pours out. Jesus, the obedient Son in a garden, reverses Adam's disobedience in Eden.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Shepherd struck for the sheep, the obedient Son who drinks the cup of judgment in our place, and the willing sacrifice who could call twelve legions of angels but lays down His life to fulfill the Scriptures.
basic.god: The Father's will is the cross, and the Son submits to it in love. God ordains the suffering foretold by the prophets, and He is powerful to rescue yet purposes salvation through the surrender of His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 13 gives the struck Shepherd. Isaiah 51 and Jeremiah 25 give the cup of God's wrath. Hebrews 5 recalls Jesus' loud cries and prayers. Philippians 2 shows His obedience unto death.
basic.oneStory: In a garden, where the first man grasped his own will and fell, the last Adam surrenders His will to the Father and takes up the cup that fell should have poured on us. Struck as the Shepherd so the scattered sheep might be gathered, Jesus goes willingly to His arrest, fulfilling the Scriptures. The story moves toward the cross where the cup is drunk to the dregs, and the obedience of Gethsemane secures the salvation Eden lost.

context.literary:
This passage is the hinge between the Supper and the trial, and Matthew builds it in three movements that each hold two sides of Jesus' night in view. In verses 31 to 35 Jesus speaks and the disciples answer with confident promises. In verses 36 to 46 Jesus prays three times and returns three times to find them asleep. In verses 47 to 56 the crowd arrives and the disciples, who promised so much, flee. The sequence moves from words to prayer to action, and in each part what the disciples say and do is set against what Jesus does.

Threes run through the account. Peter will deny three times, verse 34. Jesus prays three times, verses 39, 42 and 44, and each time He finds the three closest disciples asleep. The pattern is exact enough to be deliberate, and it contrasts the one who stays awake in prayer with the ones who cannot stay awake for an hour. Matthew also shows Jesus' obedience in the very wording of the prayers, since the second prayer shifts from 'if it is possible' to 'may Your will be done,' as though He has moved from asking to accepting.

The garden also frames the passage with a sequence of promises and fulfilments. Jesus quotes Scripture in verse 31, 'it is written,' and again in verses 54 and 56, 'the Scriptures be fulfilled,' 'the writings of the prophets.' The disciples' flight is therefore not only a failure but a fulfilment of what was written, and Matthew tells it that way to say that even the scattering is under the Father's hand. And the promise of verse 32, 'after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee,' is the only thing said about the future in the whole scene, and it is the promise that is kept in 28:7 and 28:16.

The mood is also set by the contrast of speech and silence. The disciples speak boldly in the first scene and say nothing in the second, and in the third the only speaker apart from Jesus is Judas, whose words are a lie. By the end every voice has been silenced except Jesus'.
context.historical:
The meal had ended with the Hallel and the company crossed the Kidron Valley, east of the temple, to the Mount of Olives, where there was an olive grove. The name Gethsemane is usually explained as 'oil press,' which suits a place of olive trees on the hillside, and John adds that Jesus often met His disciples there, so that Judas knew where to look, John 18:1-2. The Mount of Olives lay just outside the city, and the grove was a short walk from the upper room.

The arrest party was sent 'from the chief priests and elders,' verse 47, and carried swords and clubs. John's account adds that it included a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, with lanterns and torches, John 18:3. Judas was acting as a guide, and a kiss was a normal greeting between a disciple and a rabbi. It was this ordinary sign of respect that he chose to mark Jesus out in the dark, which is exactly why it seemed so shocking. Proverbs 27:6 says that 'the kisses of an enemy are deceitful,' and Joab's kiss of Amasa in 2 Samuel 20:9-10 had shown long before how a kiss could cover a knife.

A legion in Rome's army was nominally about six thousand men, so 'more than twelve legions of angels' means something like seventy-two thousand and more. Jesus' remark is meant to measure the contrast with the party that came for Him. The disciples' swords were two at most, Luke 22:38, He says that He could ask for an army and that the army would come at once.

Arrests at night were irregular. Jesus points out that He had sat teaching in the temple every day and could have been taken openly, verse 55. The decision to seize Him in the dark, in a garden, and away from the crowds fits the leaders' concern in verse 5 of the same chapter about a riot. The word Jesus uses for the type of person such a force comes for, 'outlaw,' is the word for a bandit or revolutionary, and it was used of the two men crucified beside Him.
context.canonical:
The scene is full of the Old Testament. Jesus' quotation in verse 31 is from Zechariah 13:7: 'Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' In Zechariah the Shepherd is 'the man who is My Companion' and the sword is the LORD's own, which shows that this is no accident. The cup of verse 39 is the cup of God's judgment in the prophets, Isaiah 51:17, 22 and Jeremiah 25:15-16, a cup of wrath that makes nations stagger. The anguish of the prayer draws on the Psalms: 'My soul is consumed with sorrow,' perilypos, echoes the refrain of Psalm 42:5, 11 and 43:5, 'Why are you downcast, O my soul?'

The Mount of Olives and the Kidron carry memories of an earlier king. David fled from his own son Absalom across the Kidron and went up the Mount of Olives weeping with his head covered, 2 Samuel 15:23, 30, and he was told that his counsellor Ahithophel was among the conspirators, 2 Samuel 15:31. Ahithophel later hanged himself, 2 Samuel 17:23. The story of the betrayed king on the Mount of Olives with a traitorous friend is one of the great background stories to this night, and Judas will end in the same way, Matthew 27:5.

The rest of the New Testament reflects on the scene. Hebrews 5:7-8 says that in His earthly days Jesus 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence. Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered.' Philippians 2:8 says He 'became obedient to death, even death on a cross.' John 18:11 records the line 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' Luke 22:43-44 adds an angel and the anguished sweat like drops of blood, and Mark 14:36 preserves the cry 'Abba, Father.' Paul's phrase that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, looks back on this night.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wrote Gethsemane for a church that knew suffering and knew failure. It shows that Jesus Himself did not walk into the cross without a struggle. He is 'deeply distressed,' He asks His friends to stay with Him, and He prays for another way. A church that was persecuted needed to know that its Lord understood anguish from the inside. Hebrews draws the same conclusion, that we have a high priest who sympathises with our weakness, Hebrews 4:15.

He also meant readers to see that the cross is an act of obedience. The refrain 'not as I will, but as You will' shows a will freely submitted to the Father, and the refusal to call on angels shows that the arrest is not something that overpowered Him. In the later words of John, He lays down His life of His own accord, John 10:18. The cross, in Matthew's telling, is chosen love and not defeat.

The disciples' behaviour is told without softening. Peter's vow, the sleepy watchmen, the sword and the flight are all there. Matthew's purpose is not to shame them but to show the need of a Saviour whose faithfulness does not depend on theirs, and to prepare readers for the restoration promised in verse 32. The story of the failure is also told so that later disciples will not be surprised by their own weakness, and will 'watch and pray' in earnest.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The scene is a narrative, and most of it is description. Jesus' three-time prayer and His distress record what happened that night, and they are not a formula that every believer must pray three times or feel the same depth of sorrow. His prayer is not a pattern for bargaining with God, either, since He asks and then yields. What carries forward is the shape of the prayer: honest about the cost, 'let this cup pass from Me,' and surrendered in the end, 'not as I will, but as You will.' This is why it matches the Lord's Prayer, 'Your will be done,' 6:10.

Jesus' words to the disciples are also commands that apply to us: 'Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation,' verse 41. His word to the man with the sword, 'Put your sword back in its place,' is addressed to a particular disciple in a particular moment, and Jesus' reason, that those who take up the sword die by it, and that He could ask for angels, shows that His kingdom is not advanced by the violence of His followers. It should not be turned into either a blanket rule on every use of force or a justification for it. Christian traditions have drawn different conclusions about the state's use of force, but all must hear this scene's rebuke of those who would defend Christ by violence.

debates.question: What was the 'cup' that so distressed Jesus?

views.label: The wrath of God against sin, borne in our place
views.case: In the prophets the cup is the cup of God's fury, Isaiah 51:17 and Jeremiah 25:15-16, which makes nations stagger. Jesus speaks of the cup He is 'going to drink,' 20:22, and of drinking the cup the Father has given, John 18:11. On this reading the horror was not only death but bearing the judgment of God for sin, as Paul says He was made 'to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. This is the classic reformed reading.

views.label: The suffering and death of the cross
views.case: Others stress the physical and mental terror of the torture and death that He saw ahead, and the rejection by His own people. The Gospels use 'cup' for suffering, as in Matthew 20:22, where James and John are told they will drink it too, and so they cannot mean the full wrath of God.

views.label: A conflict with the powers of darkness
views.case: Some emphasise that Jesus tells the arresting party that 'this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness,' Luke 22:53, and see Gethsemane as a decisive moment of the long conflict with Satan that began in the wilderness. The anguish would then be the cost of resisting temptation at its most extreme.

debates.bearing: The views overlap rather than compete. Whatever the precise content of the cup, it was the cost of the cross, and Jesus' request shows that it was dreadful and His acceptance shows that it was chosen. What is shared between them is the claim that Jesus faced it for others.

debates.question: Did Jesus' human will differ from the Father's?

views.label: Two wills in one person, human and divine, in harmony
views.case: The church formally taught at the Third Council of Constantinople, in AD 681, that Christ has two natural wills, divine and human, and that the human will follows the divine freely and without opposition. Gethsemane is the main text: His human will naturally shrinks from death, and yet it freely submits. 'Not as I will, but as You will' shows a real human will obeying.

views.label: A single will whose struggle was a real temptation
views.case: Some read the prayer as a real struggle within one will to choose. They note Hebrews 4:15, that He was 'tempted in every way, just as we are, yet without sin,' and Hebrews 5:7-8, that He learned obedience through what He suffered, as the sign that the struggle was genuine and not an act.

debates.bearing: Both views insist that the humanity is real and the obedience is sinless. The prayer is neither a pretence nor a contest between the Son and the Father; it is the Son's freely chosen agreement with the Father's plan, at a cost.

debates.question: How should 'Friend, do what you came for' be read?

views.label: A command or permission
views.case: The BSB reads it as a statement, and the sense is that Jesus invites Judas to carry out his purpose. It fits the Lord's control of events: He is not seized unawares but gives leave.

views.label: A question or an unfinished sentence
views.case: The Greek is compressed, and some read it as a question, 'Friend, why have you come?' or as an unfinished sentence. On this reading Jesus is making a last appeal to the man who has come with a kiss.

debates.bearing: Either way, Jesus calls Judas 'Friend' and does not curse him. He gives Judas a final opportunity to see what he is doing, and the following events show that he refused it.

study.originalLanguages:
Jesus says in verse 31 that the disciples will 'fall away,' skandalisthesesthe, the verb for being tripped by a skandalon, a trap or a stumbling block. It is the same verb that Matthew used for those who fall away when trouble comes, 13:21, and that the Olivet Discourse used of the many who will fall away in the tribulation, 24:10. Jesus announces it as a fact about that night, and Peter's reply 'I never will,' verse 33, is built on the same verb in the negative. The promise is made in a mood of certainty, and Jesus answers with the equally certain word that the cock will crow, alektor, before the denial.

In verse 37 Matthew says that Jesus began 'to be sorrowful and deeply distressed,' lypeisthai kai ademonein. The second verb, ademoneo, conveys a heavy, confused distress, a shuddering dismay, and it appears for Jesus in this scene in Mark also. Jesus then says, 'My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death,' perilypos estin he psyche mou heos thanatou. The adjective perilypos means surrounded by grief, and it is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in the refrain of Psalm 42:5 and 11, 'Why are you downcast, O my soul?' Jesus takes the psalmist's cry onto His own lips, and so the one who answered the psalmist by hoping in God does the same.

He falls 'facedown,' epesen epi prosopon autou, the posture of the most reverent supplication, and prays 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass,' poterion. The word is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for the cup of God's wrath in Isaiah 51:17 and Jeremiah 25:15. His conditional 'if it is possible' is a real petition and not a rhetorical device. Mark adds the Aramaic address, 'Abba,' Mark 14:36.

The second prayer, verse 42, says 'may Your will be done,' genetheto to thelema sou, which is the same wording as the petition of the Lord's Prayer in 6:10. The Teacher who instructed His disciples to pray 'Your will be done' now prays it Himself at the greatest cost. The Greek word thelema is the term for what one wishes or intends, and the distinction in verse 39 between 'what I will,' thelo, and 'what You will,' is grammatically balanced and not a contest.

The command 'watch and pray,' gregoreite kai proseuchesthe, verse 41, uses the same verb as the Olivet Discourse's 'keep watch' in 24:42 and 25:13, and the warning 'so that you will not enter into temptation,' peirasmon, recalls the line in the Lord's Prayer, 'lead us not into temptation,' 6:13. Jesus says that 'the spirit is willing, but the body is weak,' pneuma prothymon he de sarx asthenes, using sarx, flesh, for human frailty, which is exactly what Peter's boast has just shown.

The hour is 'near,' engiken he hora, verse 45, and the Son of Man is 'betrayed,' paradidotai, into the hands of sinners. Verse 50 has Jesus call Judas 'Friend,' hetaire, a word that Matthew alone uses, in the parable of the workers, 20:13, in the parable of the man without wedding clothes, 22:12, and here. In each case it is a polite address to someone about to be confronted with his own failure. The words 'do what you came for,' eph ho parei, are an unusually brief clause that can be taken as a command or as a question, as the debate above explains.

Jesus describes the crowd's treatment of Him as that of an outlaw, lestes, verse 55, which is the word for a bandit or violent revolutionary, and used of the two men crucified with Him, 27:38. In verse 56 the disciples 'deserted Him,' aphentes auton, literally they left Him, a form of the verb for forgiving and leaving behind, aphiemi, and 'fled,' ephygon. The sentence ends with the verb of flight, and the only thing that stands after it is the arrest and the trial.

typology.type: The struck Shepherd and scattered sheep, Zechariah 13:7
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah calls on the sword to awake 'against My Shepherd, against the man who is My Companion,' and says 'Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' Jesus applies the verse to the night He is arrested, and it is fulfilled exactly when the disciples flee in verse 56. The escalation is that the Shepherd is not an anonymous figure but the Son, and the striking is the Father's act, as Isaiah says, 'it was the LORD's will to crush Him,' Isaiah 53:10. The scattering is also not the last word, because Jesus adds that He will go ahead of them into Galilee, verse 32, so the gathering follows the striking. The type falls short of the reality only in its scale, since Zechariah's shepherd struck for the sake of Israel and Jesus is struck for many.

typology.type: The cup of wrath, Isaiah 51:17 and Jeremiah 25:15
typology.fulfillment: In the prophets the cup is what God hands to rebellious people, and it makes them stagger and fall. Isaiah 51:17 says Jerusalem has 'drained the goblet to the dregs,' and in the same chapter, 51:22, God says He will take the cup from her hand. Jesus takes the cup in her place. The correspondence is that He drinks what was meant for others, as the First Letter of Peter puts it, 'the righteous for the unrighteous,' 1 Peter 3:18. The escalation is that the cup now passes from the people to the one who has done no wrong, and Isaiah's promise to take it away from the sufferer is fulfilled by His drinking it. The picture falls short at only one point, since the cup was drunk in a single night and a single afternoon and its effects continue forever.

typology.type: The last Adam in a garden
typology.fulfillment: The first Adam was placed in a garden and failed to obey, and the result was exile and death, Genesis 3. In a garden across the Kidron the second man falls on His face and submits. Paul calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come,' Romans 5:14, and says that 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. The correspondence is the place, a garden, the question of obedience and the stakes. The contrast is striking, since the first Adam hid among the trees when God came looking, and the last Adam, who knows that the betrayer is coming, says 'Rise, let us go,' verse 46. Matthew does not name Adam here, so the link is an echo, though Paul's teaching makes it a fair one.

typology.type: David on the Mount of Olives, 2 Samuel 15
typology.fulfillment: David, the anointed king, left the city by way of the Kidron and climbed the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered, because his own son had rebelled and his counsellor Ahithophel had joined the conspiracy, 2 Samuel 15:23, 30, 31. Jesus, the Son of David, leaves the city the same way on the night that His friend turns against Him, and Judas, like Ahithophel, ends by hanging himself, 2 Samuel 17:23 and Matthew 27:5. The correspondence is the route, the grief and the betrayal by a trusted man. The escalation is that David was fleeing to save himself and returned to his throne, while Jesus goes toward the cross and gains His throne through it. The Gospels do not state the link outright, so it is an echo, but the geography makes it hard to miss.

study.christ:
Gethsemane shows Christ in His humanity as nowhere else. The Son of God, who has healed the sick and calmed the storm, falls on His face and says that His soul is 'consumed with sorrow to the point of death.' He does not hide it from His friends. He asks Peter, James and John, the three who saw Him in glory on the mountain, 17:1, to stay awake with Him, and they cannot. The Gospel that began with the genealogy and the virgin birth shows here that the incarnation is complete: He can be afraid, He can be lonely, and He can need His friends. This is why Hebrews says He is able to sympathise with our weaknesses, Hebrews 4:15.

He is also the obedient Son. Matthew shows the prayer in three stages. 'If it is possible' states the request, 'Yet not as I will, but as You will' states the surrender, and the second and third prayers, 'may Your will be done,' show surrender as a settled stance. Where Adam grasped, Christ yields. Where Israel in the wilderness grumbled and tested God, the true Israel obeys. In Paul's words, 'He humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8. And Hebrews says that 'although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8, which describes Gethsemane well. The Son always obeyed; at the cross, the obedience was tested in the extreme.

He is the Shepherd who is struck. The quotation of Zechariah makes the cross God's own act as well as men's, because the sword is the LORD's. The Shepherd takes the blow so that the sheep may live, and the promise that He will go ahead of them into Galilee shows that the scattered flock will be regathered by the same Shepherd. John records that the good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. The disciples' failure is no obstacle to this, since He knows it in advance and names it, and He promises to meet them again.

He is the one who willingly goes. 'Are you not aware that I can call on My Father, and He will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels?' verse 53. The rescue was available, and He declined it. This is not weakness. The disciple who drew a sword was trying to prevent what Jesus had decided to accept. The arrest is the moment when the King lets Himself be bound, and Jesus' control is evident in the way He directs events, rebuking Peter, healing the servant's ear as Luke records, Luke 22:51, and speaking to the crowd as their equal rather than as a captive.

He is the one who fulfils the Scriptures. Twice in this passage He says that what is happening is the fulfilment of 'the Scriptures' and 'the writings of the prophets,' verses 54 and 56. The Old Testament was not a set of predictions He happened to match, but a plan that He took up and carried out. He interprets His arrest, His abandonment and His death by the prophets.

And He is the friend who is faithful to the unfaithful. He tells Peter his denial in advance, but also says that He will go ahead of them into Galilee. He calls Judas 'Friend.' He shows no bitterness at His sleeping disciples, but only the gentle truth that 'the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.' The One who went into the garden alone is the same One who will meet the ones who left Him, and who will say to them on the mountain in Galilee, 'I am with you always,' 28:20.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that His plan includes the cross. 'But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?' verse 54. The striking of the Shepherd is a plan found in the prophets, and the Father's hand is in it. Isaiah says it was 'the LORD's will to crush Him,' Isaiah 53:10. This does not make the Father cruel, nor the Son a reluctant victim. The Father gives His Son, Romans 8:32, and the Son gives Himself, Galatians 2:20. The whole Trinity is at work in the same act, a unity of purpose in which the Son's 'not as I will' is the answer of love to love.

He is a God who listens and does not always grant the request in the way it is asked. Jesus prays three times for the cup to pass, and it does not pass. Hebrews says that He 'was heard because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7, which means that the answer was not removal of the cup but strength to drink it, and the angel who strengthened Him in Luke 22:43 is a sign of it. The scene teaches that unanswered is not the same as unheard, and that the Father's will, even when it costs the Son everything, is good.

He is powerful and restrained. The twelve legions of angels were available, and the Father held them back. The power that could have scattered the arresting party was held for the sake of the greater purpose. In the Old Testament God's power is seen in plagues and parted seas, but here it is seen in a man who does not resist. The weakness of Jesus in the garden is not an absence of divine power but its disciplined use.

He is a God who judges sin. The cup is the cup of God's wrath, and it is real. The Father does not ignore sin, and the Son does not make light of what He has to bear. The cost of redemption is shown by the weight of Jesus' sorrow, which proves that sin is serious, that the Father's justice is real, and that His love goes to the limit.

He is faithful in the face of human failure. Peter will deny, the disciples will flee, Judas will betray, and the plan will not fail. God does not depend on the faithfulness of His people for the fulfilment of His purposes. Yet He does not excuse them. The warning 'watch and pray' is serious, and the promise 'I will go ahead of you into Galilee' is equally sure.

For worship this means two things. The Gethsemane prayer shows us how to bring our fears honestly to God, 'if it is possible,' and then how to trust, 'Your will be done.' And it gives us a Saviour who prayed in the dark so that we could pray in the light, and who submitted to the Father's will so that we could be brought into the Father's family.

crossReferences.note: The prophecy Jesus quotes in verse 31. The sword is called upon against 'My Shepherd, against the man who is My Companion,' and the sheep are scattered. It shows that the Shepherd's striking is under God's hand and that the flock's scattering is foretold, not an accident.

Jerusalem is said to have drunk from the LORD's hand 'the cup of His fury' and drained the goblet to the dregs. This is the prophetic background of the cup in verse 39. Verse 22 of the same chapter promises that God will take the cup from her hand, which Jesus brings about by drinking it.

The LORD gives Jeremiah the cup of the wine of wrath for the nations to drink, and they 'will drink and stagger.' It confirms that the cup in Jesus' prayer is the cup of divine judgment on sin, which He takes on behalf of others.

The psalmist's refrain, 'Why are you downcast, O my soul?' is repeated in verse 11 and in Psalm 43:5. The Greek version uses the word that Jesus uses of His own soul. He takes a cry of the faithful in distress and makes it His own, and like the psalmist He ends by trusting.

David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping with his head covered, after hearing that his counsellor Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy. Jesus goes to the same mountain on the night one of His own turns against Him, and Ahithophel's end, 2 Samuel 17:23, is mirrored by Judas'.

The writer sums up Gethsemane. Jesus offered prayers 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence.' He learned obedience through suffering. It confirms that the struggle was real and that the obedience was perfect.

Paul says that Christ, though in the form of God, emptied Himself and 'became obedient to death, even death on a cross.' Gethsemane is where that obedience is spoken aloud, and the passage shows that the Son's submission is not a lessening of His deity but an expression of His love.

John names Peter as the one who drew the sword and Malchus as the servant, and gives Jesus' words, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' It shows how Jesus connected the cup of the garden to the arrest and why He told Peter to put the sword away.

Only Luke records that an angel strengthened Jesus and that His sweat became like drops of blood. It underlines the intensity of the struggle and shows that the Father's answer to the prayer was strength, not removal of the cup.

Mark preserves the Aramaic 'Abba, Father' and adds 'all things are possible for You.' It shows the intimacy of Jesus' address, and it makes the surrender more striking: the one who knows that nothing is impossible for the Father still says 'not what I will, but what You will.'

Paul says that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' It looks back on the night of Gethsemane and shows its meaning for believers. If the Father gave up the Son, He will not withhold anything else we need.

The Lord's Prayer contains 'Your will be done' and 'lead us not into temptation.' Both appear again in Gethsemane, where Jesus prays the first and tells His disciples to pray against the second. The prayer He taught is the prayer He prays in the dark.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story turns on two gardens. In Eden the first man was given everything and was asked to trust a single word, and he took what was forbidden. The result was exile, with a sword at the gate and a curse on the ground. In Gethsemane the last Adam is given a cup He did not want, and He takes what the Father has given. The first man's will was set against God's and brought death; the second man's will is yielded to God's and brings life. The whole history of sin and redemption is held in the contrast between the two gardens.

The scene also gathers the story of Israel. The nation was the Lord's flock, scattered by bad shepherds and led into exile, as Ezekiel and Zechariah said. The promise was that God Himself would come to shepherd them, and that a faithful Shepherd would be struck and the flock scattered, and then gathered again. This night is where that promise comes to pass. The Shepherd is struck at His arrest, the sheep scatter at once, and the reunion promised in verse 32 is kept in the Galilean mountain at the end of the Gospel.

What happens in the garden is also the hinge of the whole plan of salvation. The cup that the prophets said would be drunk by the nations is taken by the One who has done no wrong, so that the rest may be spared. The long line of sacrifices, from Abel's lamb to the Passover to the temple, comes to the point where the real sacrifice offers Himself. Abraham once bound his beloved son on a mountain and was told not to go through with it, and God provided a ram, Genesis 22. Now the Father does not spare His own Son, Romans 8:32, and no substitute is provided other than the Son Himself.

The disciples' failure also belongs to the story. God's people are weak, and the story has never relied on their strength. The call 'watch and pray' will be heard again in the letters to the churches, and the way of restoration, the Galilean meeting after the resurrection, shows that failure is not the end. The disciples who fled will become the witnesses sent into all the world.

The new creation turns on this night. Because the Son drank the cup, there is no more curse, and the tree of life is open, Revelation 22:2-3. The one who prayed alone in the garden is the one who will wipe every tear from the eyes of His people, Revelation 21:4, and the garden where the Son surrendered becomes the city where God and His people dwell together. What Eden lost, Gethsemane begins to win back.

quiz.q: What was the heart of Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane?

options.text: Surrender to the Father's will: not as I will, but as You will.
options.note: Verses 39 and 42 center the prayer on submission to the Father's will.

options.text: A request that the cup be taken from Him.
options.note: He did ask this, but always subordinated it to the Father's will, which is the deeper point.

options.text: A demand that God rescue Him from His enemies.
options.note: He refused rescue; He submitted rather than demanding deliverance.

options.text: A prayer that His disciples would stay awake.
options.note: He asked them to watch, but His own prayer was submission to the Father's will.

quiz.q: What does the cup Jesus prayed about most fully represent?

options.text: The cup of God's judgment against sin, which He would drink in the place of sinners.
options.note: The prophetic cup of wrath best explains His agony and the atonement.

options.text: The physical pain of crucifixion He was about to endure.
options.note: It includes His suffering, but the cup carries the deeper sense of bearing God's judgment, which this omits.

options.text: A test of whether He would stay loyal to the disciples.
options.note: The cup concerns His mission to bear judgment, not loyalty to the disciples.

options.text: A symbol of the Passover wine at the Supper.
options.note: This cup is the cup of judgment He must drink, not the Passover cup.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus refuse to be defended by the sword?

options.text: He could summon legions of angels, but chose to fulfill the Scriptures and drink the cup.
options.note: Verses 52-54 show His deliberate choice to let Scripture be fulfilled.

options.text: He wanted to avoid unnecessary violence at His arrest.
options.note: He did rebuke the sword, but the deeper reason was to fulfill the Scriptures, not merely to avoid violence.

options.text: He had no power to resist those who came for Him.
options.note: He explicitly could call twelve legions of angels; His surrender was chosen, not forced.

options.text: The disciples had told Him not to resist.
options.note: A disciple drew a sword to defend Him; Jesus overruled that, choosing the cross.

quiz.q: How does Matthew present Jesus in His arrest?

options.text: As the willing, sovereign Son fulfilling the Scriptures, not a helpless victim.
options.note: His refusal of angels and appeal to Scripture show His willing sovereignty.

options.text: As a righteous man overpowered by His enemies.
options.note: He is seized, but Matthew stresses His choice and control, which this misses.

options.text: As someone caught off guard by the betrayal.
options.note: He foretold the betrayal and met it knowingly, calling Judas friend.

options.text: As a rebel resisting arrest by force.
options.note: He stopped the sword and submitted peacefully.

questions: Jesus told His friends to watch and pray so they would not fall into temptation, yet they slept. Where is prayerful watchfulness the very thing you are neglecting before a testing time?
In agony Jesus still prayed, not as I will, but as You will. What would it look like to pray that honest prayer over the hardest thing you are facing?
Peter was sure he would never fall. Where might your confidence in your own faithfulness actually be a warning sign?
Jesus drank the cup of judgment so you would never have to. How does that reshape the way you face your own suffering, knowing the worst cup has already been drained for you?
Jesus could have called legions of angels but chose the cross for you. How does His willing surrender move your worship and your obedience today?

translationNotes.note: The quotation is Zechariah 13:7, I will strike the Shepherd and the sheep will be scattered; presented here as prose for a clean reading and applied to that very night.
The cup echoes the prophetic cup of God's wrath (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15); Jesus prays for its removal yet submits to the Father, embracing it in the sinner's place.
Friend, do what you came for may also be rendered Friend, for what have you come; either way Jesus meets the betrayal knowingly and with sober composure.
